new_statements.relation_note: Catalog: Kolami fixed: initial syllable (strict) from Emeneau 1955:8 sec. 2.10 ('The first syllable of a word has a stress accent of medium intensity'). Krishnamurti 2003:27 states initial, non-phonemic stress for all Dravidian languages, Kolami among them (his Kolami sources are Sethumadhava Rao 1950 and Emeneau 1955b) -> same placement and type; adds the family-level nuance that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (a mild refinement, not Kolami-specific, so recorded as agrees rather than refines). No Kolami-specific statement could be read because ch. 2 pp. 48-77 is not yet obtained and has no open copy; the Google index of the book shows no Kolami stress passage.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide typological statement covering all Dravidian languages treated (Kolami included as language 19): stress is non-phonemic; loudness normally falls on the word-initial syllable regardless of its length; a long vowel in a non-initial syllable is louder than short vowels (i.e. attracts some prominence). No Kolami-specific stress paragraph is held: sec. 2.4.1 (p. 59), reached only as Google Books snippets by the compilers, quotes statements for Tamil, Telugu (Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991) and Konda; Google Books feed queries for 'Kolami' + 'stress' / 'initial syllable' restricted to this volume return 0 entries (control query '"phonemic stress"' returns the p. 27 snippet from this volume), so the book's searchable text appears to contain no Kolami-specific stress sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such on p. 27; only 'A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (non-initial long vowels carry extra loudness). Sec. 2.4.1 snippets mention 'secondary stress' for Tamil/Telugu examples only (not held in full).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kolami. The p. 27 rule is hedged with 'Normally'; non-initial long vowels louder than short vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti treats Kolami as language 19 (Kōlāmī; Adilabad district of Andhra Pradesh, Yeotmal and Wardha districts of Maharashtra), Central Dravidian, with Naikri (20a) and Naiki of Chanda (20b) as separate related languages; his Kolami sources are Sethumadhava Rao 1950 and Emeneau 1955b (Wardha dialect). The stress statement read is family-wide (Proto-/pan-Dravidian typological profile), not a description of a Kolami variety.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The fixed: initial syllable (fixed-strict) coding rests on the standard reference grammar (Emeneau 1955, UCPL 12, 302 pp.), which we hold in full and whose deciding passage (p. 8 section 2.10) plus three corroborating loci (2.4, 2.13, 2.37) I confirmed verbatim in the held scanned. Emeneau's statement is unambiguous: first-syllable stress, mechanically placeable, with vowel-length contrast licensed only in the accented initial syllable. No better or later dedicated source on Kolami prosody exists in Glottolog's bibliography or in the Semantic Scholar/Crossref/archive. Two open items downloaded now (Sjoberg 1971 ERIC report; Grierson LSI extract) are silent on Kolami specifically. Intonations and junctures. The material is too slight to allow an exact analysis. [...] So far as my observation went, all sections between silences have the same intonation pattern. Its chief feature is that all syllables, accented and unaccented, are on about the same pitch level,* except that the last syllable of a section, if unaccented, is on a slightly higher pitch. [footnote:] *This statement may be inexact, but my impression is that it is not very far wrong.
